what: CORRECTION to entry #5 (and to my earlier chat summary): I said the first failure was the network collapsing onto a single direction. That mechanism was not measured. What was measured: without the correlation penalty the run fails (slow-block R2 0.43, 7 of 8 output directions still active); with it, it works (R2 0.99). plain.did: Ran the authors' simulation script exactly as published, on the same 5 seeds, and put its numbers beside ours.
output: Paper's SplitJEPA, run by the authors' script, 5 seeds (ours in brackets):
Paper's LeJEPA baseline (no spectral head), same script:
invariant_r2 0.9619 ± 0.0327 (ours without spectral head: 0.486 ± 0.080)
global_r2 0.9977 ± 0.0016 (identical to SplitJEPA, as in the paper)
Their script reproduces the paper's table, so the paper's claim holds when we run it.
Our gap: about 0.01 lower on the R² scores. Leakage (a12, a21) and block purity are about the same.
Cause of the small gap is not isolated: our encoder is a generic network on 16 observed numbers, theirs mirrors the scrambling function on 8.
plain.relevance: Closes Stage A's cross-check. Our pipeline recovers the invariant block almost as well as the authors' own code, which is solid ground to build the second split on. The paper's LeJEPA baseline is much stronger than ours (0.96 vs 0.49) because of their encoder design, so comparisons against 'before' numbers must say which encoder was used.

plain.relevance: Tells us whether the gap is our encoder choice or something in our pipeline. If it is only the encoder, Stage B can use our generic encoder with confidence; if not, we fix the pipeline first.
